episode.episode: Philips Hue: The smart home’s light bulb moment
episode.showDescription: Version History is a show about the best gadgets ever. And the worst ones. And the ones that might have changed the world, if they ever actually shipped. Every week, your favorite people from The Verge and beyond hang out to tell and debate the story of a gadget, app, website, or any other tech product, and try to determine the item’s true legacy. Because not every product is a hit, but every product has a story. And the ones that really matter aren’t always the ones you think. From the Verge and the Vox Media Podcast Network.
episode.episodeDescription: The humble light bulb might be the ultimate success story in the smart home. Our connected, adaptable homes are supposed to be customizable, connected to everything, and incredibly easy to use, and nothing has made that work quite like Philips Hue lights. In this episode, The Verge's David Pierce and Jennifer Pattison Tuohy are joined by smart home journalist and expert Richard Gunther to tell the Hue's story. We trace the product's history from its origins in the smartphone revolution, try to figure out how Philips managed to turn a staggeringly expensive lightbulb into a must-have gadget, and look at whether there's even more invention left in the future of lighting. We’re also on video! Check us out on YouTube. Subscribe to The Verge for unlimited access to theverge.com, subscriber-exclusive newsletters, and our ad-free podcast feed. We love hearing from you! transcript_window.text: A number of companies have tried to do this, I would argue, largely unsuccessfully.
Every time somebody tries to come up with a creative new spin on the light switch, I just kind of wince a little bit.

There's a bunch of folks in this space who refer to poorly designed light switches as Gunther switches, I have such an issue with poorly ergonomically designed light Don't going on the GE Sync switches.
Oh.
This is a great thing to be known for.
People being mad at their light switches, associating them with you, I think is what a great legacy that And after me.
Yeah.
It's an honor.
For sure.
No, I would have loved that.
And, I mean, you could argue that Sonos sort of went down that same path, creating their own remotes for their system, up just reverting back to the phone.
Yeah, that's very true.
We all did converge back there, right or wrong.
That's where we landed.

Well, and that was a really interesting part of this history, which I hadn't really realized, I suppose, at the time, because I was only just starting to cover smart home when Hugh launched, was that it was the first smart home interface for the iPhone.
Like Apple had not even, well, who knows?
knows, Apple maybe had considered, but they hadn't said anything publicly about how this could be used to control devices in your home.
And this was kind of like the beginning of the smartphone based smart home.
So you can all blame Hugh.
I think that's right.
And I think for reasons we will get to, I think there's a pretty strong case to be made that Apple, in fact, had not thought about this at all.
And I think in general, what's happening at this time is everyone is discovering things for the smartphone to be for.
Right.
This idea that I have an always connected, logged in, camera filled, location based object in my pocket is changing everything at like record speed.
And this is just one version of that.
But so this team starts building.
